text: NextAuth.js deployments always expose /api/auth/providers unauthenticated by design — immediately enumerate all provider callback URLs as OAuth redirect attack surfaces in wave 1 auth testing
When backend hostname is exposed via CSP connect-src, enumerate beyond /health — probe /api, /v1, /v2, /docs, /swagger, /openapi.json unauthenticated before assuming full auth protection

Azure Container Apps environment names in hostnames (livelystone) can be used to enumerate sibling apps — other containers in the same environment may share the livelystone-c1480484.westus2.azurecontainerapps.io namespace

Dev environment returning env:production from /health is a misconfiguration signal — dev and prod may share the same backend container image/config, meaning dev environment has full production data access

Pusher WebSocket integrations require a backend channel authorization endpoint — probe /pusher/auth, /api/pusher/auth, and /realtime/auth before any authenticated session is obtained to check unauthenticated channel subscription
Payment subdomain (pay.copointdata.com) resolved but timed out — dedicated subdomain takeover and tech-stack fingerprinting wave needed before payment-specific auth and data access testing

Next.js /_next/static/ JS bundles contain client-side route definitions, API paths, and occasionally leaked secrets — always enumerate and fetch main chunks for API surface mapping before auth testing

CSP nonces observed to rotate per-request on /login — XSS via script injection is blocked at the CSP layer; focus XSS testing on DOM-based sinks and non-script injection vectors (iframe, meta refresh, object)

CORS headers present on backend but Access-Control-Allow-Origin not captured — always capture CORS preflight response in wave 1 to determine if credentials-bearing cross-origin requests are allowed from arbitrary origins
v0.dev AI-generated UIs tend to implement client-side validation only — prioritize server-side input validation testing on all form fields and API parameters in post-auth waves

CORS wildcard-with-credentials is now confirmed critical across ALL backend routes — any XSS, postMessage injection, or DOM sink that enables script execution from an attacker origin gives full credentialed API read/write access. Prioritize finding ANY XSS vector in wave 2 even if CSP blocks script-injection, as non-script sinks (iframe srcdoc, blob: URL, data: URL, SVG onload) bypass CSP nonces.

OIDC nonce absence (f_b7d42a8c) must be validated via active Azure AD flow — open a real OAuth session, capture the id_token JWT, attempt replay with modified sub/email claims. If NextAuth does not reject replayed id_tokens, account takeover is possible for any user whose email is known.

RBAC IDOR (f_g8c47e5b) on /rbac/users/{id}/role requires authenticated testing. Pattern: authenticate as low-privilege user, enumerate role IDs via /rbac/roles (GET), attempt PUT/POST to /rbac/users/{own_id}/role with admin role ID. Server-side authorization check for self-role-escalation is the key missing validation.

Azure Container Apps backend on livelystone-c1480484.westus2.azurecontainerapps.io should be probed for IMDS metadata endpoint access (http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance and http://169.254.169.254/metadata/identity/oauth2/token) — managed identity token from IMDS would give Azure AD Graph access and potential lateral movement to other Azure resources.

The null-origin CORS reflection (f_a3c9e1f2) enables sandboxed iframe attacks without any XSS — an attacker page can create a sandboxed iframe with srcdoc containing fetch() calls that carry null origin, and the backend will reflect it with credentials:true. This is an independent exploit path that does not require XSS.

GraphQL at /graphql is auth-gated but introspection may still be enabled for authenticated sessions. Once any authenticated session is obtained, immediately run introspection to map the full schema, identify sensitive mutations (user role changes, data deletions, billing ops), and test for broken object-level authorization in queries.

CSRF cookie is non-HttpOnly by design (double-submit pattern) — but this means the CSRF token is readable by JavaScript. Combined with CORS-with-credentials, an attacker performing a CORS-based attack already bypasses CSRF: they can read the csrf-token cookie value via CORS GET /api/auth/csrf and replay it in a subsequent credentialed POST — eliminating the CSRF protection entirely.

Pay.copointdata.com timed out in wave 0 and was not addressed in wave 1. Given the application handles CRM and revenue operations, a payment subdomain is critical-path. Dedicate a recon pass to characterize the payment subdomain tech stack and auth model before wave 3.

PostgreSQL 17.8 version disclosure via unauthenticated /api/health endpoint (f_hlth0001, f_hlth0002) enables targeted CVE lookup for the exact DB version. Wave 2 nuclei should scan for PostgreSQL-specific CVEs and check for /api/health being accessible on production (revops.copointdata.com) as well.

Git commit SHA hardcoded in Datadog telemetry (61c5fdeac36ed85a883ae93b78c06d03f9f4e4a1) — if the repository is public or the organization has public GitHub repos, this SHA may allow source code retrieval. Check github.com/copointai or similar orgs for this commit hash.

CORS null-origin exploitation is self-contained and does not require XSS — a sandboxed iframe (sandbox attribute on an attacker-hosted page) creates a null-origin context that the backend reflects with credentials:true. Wave 5 exploitation can proceed directly with a PoC HTML page without needing any XSS vector found in Wave 4.

CORS wildcard-with-credentials is confirmed on ALL backend routes including 401 responses — the CSRF double-submit pattern is completely defeated because an attacker can CORS-read /api/auth/csrf to extract the csrf-token, then replay it in a credentialed state-mutating POST. Wave 3 should enumerate all state-mutating endpoints for maximum chain impact.

GitHub leaks scan is highest-priority for Wave 3 — the Git SHA 61c5fdeac36ed85a883ae93b78c06d03f9f4e4a1 and Azure Tenant ID 9046c3d1-04fe-4afe-9e4f-9217f27b5a66 confirm a real codebase. If NEXTAUTH_SECRET or Azure client_secret is in any public repo, the entire auth stack is compromised without needing CORS exploitation.

OIDC nonce bypass (chain_003, EV=0.76) requires active live testing — the Azure AD OIDC flow must be exercised to determine if NextAuth validates the nonce claim in id_tokens. This cannot be confirmed statically. Wave 3 OSINT should surface the exact NextAuth version in use, as CVE-2023-48309 applicability depends on version.

11 SSRF-capable endpoints are auth-gated but represent a critical post-authentication attack surface for chain_006. Once any authenticated session is obtained (via CORS exploitation, leaked credentials, or OSINT social engineering), SSRF against Azure IMDS (169.254.169.254) must be the immediate next action to attempt managed identity token theft.

Supply chain analysis of Next.js and NextAuth versions is high value — the stack uses Next.js and NextAuth which have had significant CVEs (CVE-2023-48309, CVE-2024-34351, CVE-2025-29927). Exact version pins from package.json or bundle fingerprinting could confirm exploitable vulnerabilities bypassing auth entirely.

OSINT enumeration of revops.copointdata.com user base (LinkedIn, Apollo, breach databases) is critical for demonstrating real-world chain_002 impact — the null-origin CORS PoC requires a victim user to visit the attacker page. If real employee emails are known, a targeted spear-phishing delivery becomes the missing exploitation link.
CORS null-origin PoC produced and verified via curl — chain_002 is fully exploitable with social engineering delivery
All post-auth chains (SSRF→IMDS, RBAC IDOR, GraphQL authz) are conditional on chain_002 but have high EV once auth is obtained
No new post-exploit pivots discovered — proceed to report, do not loop
